Steering report

Persona-vector steering of LLM agents in multi-agent games: does it change what they say, how they play, and what happens to the group?

Key findings
  • 0 of 8 traits move significantly in the steered direction. Strongest: ; weakest: SD per unit coefficient.
  • 0 of -8 off-diagonal cells are significant: the vectors are fairly specific.
  • Prompt vs vector: for 0 of 16 trait × side cases the prompt's effect on the readout equals the vector's somewhere in the tested range (median |c| ≈ nan).
  • Group welfare, significant: all × opportunistic: -0.31; one × opportunistic: -0.17; both_one × opportunistic: -0.17; all × assertive: +0.16; all × sarcastic: -0.15; both_one × empathy: -0.14.
  • No significant contagion: the co-players' language does not shift with the steered agent's trait.
  • Pooled over games, the steered agent's reward changes for: opportunistic: -0.19; empathy: -0.10; assertive: +0.10; sarcastic: -0.09.
  • No significant effect on the deceiving side's reward.
  • Steering changes the outcome for: no trait; the readout predicts the outcome for: no trait.
Generated from the numbers below; each section explains its measure.

Takeaways

  1. The vectors steer what agents say. 0 of 8 traits move in the steered direction (median nan SD of the trait's readout per unit c); a random direction of the same size moves it nan% as much (median), so the effect is the persona direction, not just any perturbation.
  2. Behaviour moves far less than language. Per unit c the readout shifts by a median nan SD, the steered agent's own reward by at most 0.19 SD (pooled); 18 of 56 game × trait reward slopes are significant. More of the trait pays off for assertive (+0.10); it costs the agent for empathy (-0.10), opportunistic (-0.19), sarcastic (-0.09) (SD per unit c). A persona that is plainly visible in the text often leaves the agent's result unchanged (its concrete choices can still shift: section 15).
  3. The setting 'good_team' moves outcomes most. Typical size of the steered agents' reward effect per setting (median |slope| over the traits): good_team 0.08, both_one 0.07, one 0.06, all 0.05, evil_one 0.04, evil_team 0.04, good_one 0.03 SD per unit c. Group welfare (everyone's total, games without hidden roles) falls in 8 and rises in 5 significant setting × trait cells: steered groups mostly end up worse off together.
  4. A persona prompt is a close but not exact substitute for the vector. Both shift the monitored traits in a similar pattern (median cosine nan); the prompt is often as strong as the strongest vector or stronger (0 of 16 trait × sign cases beyond it). How alike they play is compared at matched strength in section 19 (takeaway 'Prompt, vector, both'). Only the vector has a strength knob, so dose–response questions need it.
  5. Steering changes concrete choices. 85 of 128 game × action × trait slopes are significant (section 15); strongest: avalon_6p (image): trustworthiness → share 'reject' -8.17; avalon_6p (image): trustworthiness → share 'approve' +4.69; avalon_6p (image): sycophantic → share 'approve' +2.94; avalon_6p: agreeableness → share 'reject' -1.87.
  6. Per setting, the zigzag is noise. Only 0 of 0 game × trait × setting reward curves depart from a straight line beyond what 32–50 episodes per point allow; the bends in the pooled game × trait curves below need all settings together to show. Where a setting moves the reward, it is mostly one-sided: 39 curves change only when pushed one way, 3 in opposite ways for the two directions, 6 the same way for both (section 16).
  7. Each vector moves a whole persona, not one trait. Over all 0 monitored personas, the steered trait moves most in only 0 of 0 cases (section 17): name a vector by its footprint, not its label.
  8. Prompt, vector, both. At matched dose the prompt moves the language more than the vector (0 of 16 trait × side cases, 0 of 0 games) and both together most (0 of 16); in play the prompt differs from the vector (r = at c = ±1, 0.71 at ±2; vector vs itself ); together they simply add (section 19).
  9. The readout is not just answer length. Controlling for length keeps most of the shift for 8 of 8 traits (section 20).
  10. Steering everyone is not the sum of steering one. The group's welfare moves about 0.8× as much as with one steered agent, far from additive; in 3 game × trait cells the all-steered group changes where one steered agent does not (e.g. gbs_6p (image) × opportunistic). One agent's own effect shrinks with group size (section 21).
  11. Hidden-role games: a whole deceiving side steered hard loses. one deceiver or one honest player steered rarely changes who wins (0 of 32 carrier comparisons differ); a trait's direction agrees across games for good_team: 2 of 2 (assertive, trustworthiness) (section 22).
  12. Image vs text, vector vs prompt. Game by game, how strongly steering moves the language carries over from text to images (slopes r = ), how it moves the result about as well (r = 0.58). The prompt moves the language SD with text and with images, the vector (c = ±1) and . On the result, prompt and vector simply add in both modes (section 25).
  13. Steering changes how much agents write. Answers average 1029 characters unsteered, 461 at c = 2 and 397 at c = -2 (section 13; per persona and setting in section 20 and in the steering mini report's recipe).
  14. Read with care: no unsteered episodes yet in harvest_5p (image), harvest_5p; over 5% of answers unparseable in gbs_6p (image) (the agent then plays a default move), so reward effects there partly reflect parsing.
What the sections add up to, written from their numbers; the evidence for each point is in the sections below.

Setup: what was run and what is measured

Modelqwen3.8-27b; every agent is the same model, generating with PersVecFast's sampling settings (Qwen3.5: temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, presence penalty 1.5, thinking off); max_tokens 1024, max_turns 200, max_parse_retries 3.SteeringvLLM-Hook's add_vector: at one decoder block, every token's hidden state becomes h + c·v, with v the raw PersVecFast persona vector of the trait (mean difference between trait-expressing and trait-suppressing answers) and c the steering coefficient. Steered and unsteered agents share one batch; each request carries its own vector. Layers: agreeableness L16, assertive L32, empathy L47, evil L32, opportunistic L47, sarcastic L47, sycophantic L47, trustworthiness L47 (the trait's best layer in PersVecFast's steering sweep).Traitsagreeableness, assertive, empathy, evil, opportunistic, sarcastic, sycophantic, trustworthinessCoefficients-2, 2 (negative = push away from the trait). Persona prompts use only the sign: + = the trait's instruction, − = its opposite.Conditions
allevery agent
all_randomevery agent gets a random direction of the same norm (control)
both_oneone agent gets the instruction AND the vector
evil_oneone member of the deceiving side
evil_teamevery member of the deceiving side (hidden-role games)
good_oneone member of the honest side
good_teamevery member of the honest side (hidden-role games)
nonenobody steered (the baseline every comparison is made against)

Games9 (game × observation mode), 35146 episodes in this report. Image mode: the game state is shown as a picture instead of text. Episode seeds depend only on the game and the episode number, so every condition plays the same deals, roles and seats.Monitor (readout): how it worksNot run for these episodes (played without the monitor engine). Every readout result (sections 2–4, 8, 11b, 14, 17, 18, 20, 23 and the readout columns elsewhere) is empty until the monitor is run over the logged turns; rewards, actions, coherence and length do not need it.OutcomeEach game's own reward for the agent (e.g. win/loss of its side in Avalon, Werewolf, Mafia; points or goods won in auctions, harvest, TextArena games). Compared paired: the same seat in the unsteered episode with the same seed (same deal, same role).StatisticsEffects are slopes per unit coefficient (a straight line through the condition's points and the unsteered agents at 0), with games as fixed effects when pooled. Standard errors are clustered by episode. * q<.05, ** q<.01, *** q<.001 after Benjamini–Hochberg correction over all cells of a table. Cell colour: red = increase, blue = decrease, stronger = more certain. Hover a cell for n, SE, p, q; '–' = not enough data.

What steering looks like: matched examples

What you seeFor each trait, games where the same seat's first answer can be compared across conditions: same game, same seed, so the agent received exactly the same prompt; the only difference is the steering. Columns: unsteered; persona vector at c = -2 and 2; a random direction of the same norm at c = 2 (control); the persona prompt (+ / −). Second row: the same seat 4 answers in (or its last, if the game is shorter), when the games have diverged: does the persona hold, fade, or derail? The number under each answer is that turn's readout of the trait (raw projection, higher = more of the trait; compare within a row). Each trait shows different games where possible, and one game played from images with the pictures the agent saw (redrawn from the episode's seed and the logged moves; shown only when the redrawn prompt matches the logged one).Why it mattersThe tables below are averages over thousands of turns; these show what a slope of the readout actually corresponds to in text, including where strong steering stops being 'more of the trait' and becomes caricature or broken output.

6. Persona prompt vs persona vector: can the prompt stand in for the vector?

QuestionIs writing the persona into the system prompt comparable to adding the persona vector — as strong, in the same direction, with the same effect on play, as visible, at the same cost?What is measuredThe same trait given as the PersVecFast instruction in the system prompt (+ = express it, − = its opposite; no strength knob) vs as the vector at c = ±0.5..±2. a: mean readout of the trait (SD vs unsteered) and the vector coefficient with the same readout (interpolated on the vector's dose-response curve). b: the shift of all 0 monitored traits as a profile; cosine 1 = same pattern, 0 = unrelated. c: paired reward (same seat, same seed, unsteered; SD units) of the one steered agent (prompt_one vs one), of the deceiving side when all its members are steered (evil_team_prompt vs evil_team), and the group's total when every agent is steered (prompt_all vs all; in hidden-role games this total only says which side won, the honest side being bigger; construction); scatter: one dot per trait × side × game. d: AUC as in section 4 and contagion as in 8 (one agent steered); answer length and unparseable answers.Games played for these results9: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), harvest_5p, harvest_5p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read it≈ vector c tells which vector strength the prompt corresponds to ('beyond' = stronger than every tested c). In the scatters, dots on the dashed diagonal = same effect; compare the prompt–vector r with the reference r (two vector strengths), which shows how well two near-identical interventions can agree given the noise. Only games run with both channels.
Result
  • Strength: for 0 of 16 trait × side cases the prompt's effect on the readout equals the vector's somewhere in the tested range (median |c| ≈ nan).
  • Behaviour: per game, the prompt's effect on the agents' reward correlates r = 0.51 with the vector's (two vector strengths agree r = , the ceiling given the noise). Clearly different pooled reward effects: agreeableness −, steered agent (prompt +0.50, vector +0.13); assertive +, steered agent (prompt -0.02, vector +0.30); empathy +, steered agent (prompt -0.05, vector -0.49); empathy −, steered agent (prompt -0.05, vector +0.30); opportunistic +, steered agent (prompt +0.14, vector -0.16); opportunistic −, steered agent (prompt +0.08, vector +0.41); sarcastic +, steered agent (prompt +0.34, vector -0.05).
  • Cost: mean answer length 863 characters with the prompt, 472 with the vector at max, 1029 unsteered.

7. Who is steered: one, half, all, one side

Who gains, who loses?What is measuredPer condition × trait, three slopes per unit coefficient: the steered agents' readout; their own reward vs the same seat in the unsteered episode with the same seed; the total reward of all agents in the episode vs the unsteered episode with the same seed.Games played for these results7: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read itRows are conditions (see Setup). 12. Text vs image observations

QuestionDoes seeing the game as a picture instead of text change how agents play at all, and does steering act differently then?What is measuredOnly games played in both modes. First the unsteered agents in each mode: their results (each seat paired with itself in the same deal, since both modes use the same seeds), unparseable answers, answer length, tokens read and generated per turn, game length. Then the steering effect: the readout slope (section 2) and the steered agent's reward slope (section 9) for text and image runs, diff = image − text; and both over the dose, text vs image.Games played for these results8: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), harvest_5p, harvest_5p (image)How to read itA significant diff means the observation format changes how strongly the persona takes hold (readout) or what it does to the agent's result (reward).
Result
  • Games played in both modes: avalon_6p, gbs_3p, gbs_6p, harvest_5p.
  • Without steering, results differ between image and text play (95% CI of the paired difference excludes 0) in 1 of 3 games (gbs_3p); unparseable answers are 4.7% with images vs 0.9% with text (mean over games); agents read 685 tokens per turn with images vs 453 with text.
  • The steered agent's result responds differently to steering with images for agreeableness (more reward per unit c), assertive (more reward per unit c) (reward table, image − text).

15. Actions: what do steered agents do differently?

QuestionBeyond the final reward: which choices change — bids, guesses and amounts, votes, play vs discard vs hint, cooperate vs defect?What is measuredEach agent's parsed choices over the episode (default moves after an unparseable answer excluded). Numeric: the mean of its numeric choices (a bid, a guess, an amount harvested; agents whose mean lies beyond 3 interquartile ranges of the game's, e.g. a guess of 10^200, are left out). Shares: the share of its choices of each type (an action label: APPROVE / REJECT, SUCCESS / FAIL, play / discard / hint, TextArena's bracketed command with numbers replaced by #, e.g. 'bid #'). Only types with ≥ 5% of the unsteered agents' choices. Steered agents with the persona vector (not the evil-side settings) against the unsteered agents at c = 0: the slope per unit c.Games played for these results7: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read itNumeric rows are in the game's own units per unit c (e.g. +12 = bids 12 coins higher per unit c); share rows in percentage points per unit c (+5 = that action 5 points more often per unit c, so +10 at c = 2). Steered seats are drawn at random, so role-specific actions (only spies can FAIL a mission) compare like with like on average. Labels are the game's own commands: single letters e.g. market entry's [S]tay / [E]nter, GOPS's card ranks A / K / Q / J; '#' = a bare number (a GOPS card value, a Mafia vote by number). Stars: Benjamini–Hochberg within each game's table.
Result
  • 85 of 128 game × action × trait slopes are significant.
  • Strongest per game: avalon_6p (image): trustworthiness → share 'reject' -8.17; avalon_6p (image): trustworthiness → share 'approve' +4.69; avalon_6p (image): sycophantic → share 'approve' +2.94; avalon_6p: agreeableness → share 'reject' -1.87; avalon_6p: sycophantic → share 'approve' +1.65; avalon_6p: sycophantic → share 'reject' -1.88; gbs_3p (image): evil → mean numeric choice +6.12; gbs_3p (image): assertive → mean numeric choice +7.43; gbs_3p (image): opportunistic → mean numeric choice +5.31; gbs_3p: evil → mean numeric choice +6.04; gbs_3p: assertive → mean numeric choice +2.62; gbs_3p: trustworthiness → mean numeric choice -2.70; gbs_6p (image): evil → mean numeric choice +7.77; gbs_6p (image): sycophantic → mean numeric choice +11.22; gbs_6p (image): assertive → mean numeric choice +11.30; 6 more.

16. Dose–response: how does the reward change with steering strength?

QuestionDoes more steering give proportionally more effect, or does the effect level off, peak at a moderate strength, or flip?What is measuredThe steered agent's reward minus the same seat's in the unsteered episode with the same seed (as in section 9), at each coefficient. Charts: all games pooled (SD units of each game's unsteered rewards), with 95% CIs. Table: per game × trait, a fit y = b₁c + b₂c² (SEs clustered by episode, Benjamini–Hochberg over the table): ↑/↓ rising/falling = only the straight part is significant; saturating = it bends back but the turning point lies beyond ±2; ∩/∪ = it peaks or dips inside the range (turning point given); flat = no significant trend. Details: the mean reward change at every coefficient, per game.Games played for these results7: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read itA ∩ means the trait helps up to a point and hurts beyond it — e.g. when moderate steering changes the play but strong steering breaks the answers (section 13). '∩ stronger either way hurts': the turning point is at c ≈ 0, so the harder the persona is pushed, in either direction, the worse the agent does. Every point is measured against the same unsteered games, so a lucky or unlucky baseline shifts the whole curve up or down: the fit has an intercept, so the shape (rising, bending) is robust to that, the level is not — with few unsteered episodes, trust shapes more than levels. Hover a table cell for the fitted coefficients. Shapes need data at ≥ 4 coefficients. Jagged lines are not a shape: with 32–50 episodes per point, the means zigzag by chance. 'Is the bend real?' tests each curve (game × trait × setting) against a straight line and against a smooth bend, given each point's SE: only curves that fail the straight line after correction really bend. 'Pushed down / up' summarises a curve without a slope: the mean change over all c < 0 and over all c > 0.
Result
  • Of 0 game × trait curves: 0 change steadily with c, 0 saturate, 0 peak or dip inside the tested range, 0 show no significant trend.
  • Is the bend real? Of 232 curves (game × trait × setting), 48 differ from 0 on at least one side; 0 of 0 depart from a straight line beyond what the per-point noise allows (0 at uncorrected p < 0.05, ≈ 0 expected by chance), 0 from a smooth bend. The zigzag in most per-setting lines is sampling noise (32–50 episodes per point), not a shape.
  • Which way of pushing matters (mean change over all c < 0 and over all c > 0 vs 0, SEs clustered by seed, BH over all sides): neither side differs from 0: 184; only pushing down helps: 13; only pushing up hurts: 10; only pushing up helps: 10; only pushing down hurts: 6; either push helps: 5; opposite ways (monotone): 3; either push hurts: 1.

The rank: where the steered trait itself comes among all personas, by movement in the steered direction.Games played for these results9: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), harvest_5p, harvest_5p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read itRank 1 = the vector's strongest effect is its own trait. A high rank means the label undersells what the vector does: read 'moved most' as its actual content. The collapsible table has every persona × vector.

19. Vector, prompt or both? Side by side

QuestionGiving an agent a persona by the vector, by the instruction in its system prompt, or by both: which moves its language more, which changes its play, which spreads to the others, which costs answer quality? The same for everyone steered and for the whole deceiving side.What is measuredOne steered agent per episode (conditions one, prompt_one, both_one). The prompt has no strength, so it is compared with the vector and with both at c = ±1 (+ = the trait's instruction / c > 0, − = its opposite / c < 0); the vector at c = ±2 for reference. Each a mean over episodes with a 95% CI (hover): b the agent's readout of its trait (SD vs unsteered agents of the same game); c its reward vs the same seat in the unsteered episode with the same seed (SD units); d unparseable answers; e answer length vs the game's unsteered answers; f the unsteered co-players' readout of the trait; g per game; h everyone steered (all vs prompt_all) and the whole deceiving side (evil_team vs evil_team_prompt); i synergy: both − (vector + prompt), all three against the same unsteered reference (0 = they add); j outcomes: significant gains and losses per arm, prompt vs vector head to head per game × trait × side, for one agent's own result and for the group when everyone is steered. Charts a: all coefficients, all games pooled.Games played for these results9: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), harvest_5p, harvest_5p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read itCompare the three arms within a row. Readout: + rows should be positive, − rows negative; a prompt cell with the wrong sign = the instruction backfires. 'both ÷ (vector + prompt)' ≈ 1: the two add; > 1 reinforce; < 1 overlap. Reward: all arms share the same unsteered reference, so differences between arms are more reliable than each value's distance from 0. Section 6 adds the direction (fingerprint), visibility and the vector strength the prompt equals.
Result
  • Strength at matched dose: the prompt moves the trait's readout further than the vector at c = ±1 for 0 of 16 trait × side cases, and at least as far as the vector at c = ±2 for 0; per game, further than the vector in 0 of 0 games (table g).
  • Both together move the readout furthest in 0 of 16 cases and in 0 of 0 games: they stack (ratio column: ≈ 1 additive, > 1 reinforcing).
  • Synergy (table i): on the readout, prompt + vector is significantly more than the sum of the two for 0 of 16 trait × side cases and less for 0; the rest add up. Per game (mean over traits and sides), more than the sum in 0 of 0 games. On the reward, the combination differs from the sum in 0 cases. A readout is a projection that can saturate, so 'less than the sum' on it can be a ceiling, not competition. These verdicts pool all games; per game, and whether the games agree: section 25e.
  • Play: per game × trait × side, the prompt's reward effect correlates r = with the vector's (n = 0); the vector at c = ±1 and at ±2 correlate r = , the most two near-identical interventions can agree given the noise. Against the vector at c = ±2 (which its readout effect resembles more) the prompt correlates r = 0.71: the prompt changes play differently. Pooled per trait × side: prompt vs vector r = , both vs vector , both vs prompt . Mean |reward change| (SD): vector nan, prompt 0.33, both nan.
  • Cost: 2.7% of turns unparseable unsteered; no arm breaks answers.
  • Contagion (co-players' readout the intended way, mean over traits and sides): vector +nan, prompt +nan, both +nan SD.
  • Outcomes, one agent steered: its own result: the prompt gives 0 significant gains and 0 losses over 0 game × trait × side cells, the vector at c = ±1 0 and 0; head to head in the same cell the prompt is better in nan% of cells, significantly better in 0 and worse in 0; its best gain in a game beats the matched vector's in 0 of 0 games. With its strength chosen per cell the vector reaches 0 significant gains (an optimistic reference: the best of several noisy strengths).
  • Outcomes, everyone steered: the group's result (games without hidden roles): the prompt gives 0 significant gains and 0 losses over 0 game × trait × side cells, the vector at c = ±1 0 and 0; head to head in the same cell the prompt is better in nan% of cells, significantly better in 0 and worse in 0; its best gain in a game beats the matched vector's in 0 of 0 games. With its strength chosen per cell the vector reaches 0 significant gains (an optimistic reference: the best of several noisy strengths).

20. Is the readout just answer length?

QuestionSteering changes how long answers are (section 13). Is the trait readout really measuring the trait, or mostly that answers got shorter or longer?What is measuredSteered agents (persona vector) and unsteered agents at c = 0, as in section 2. The readout slope over the coefficient, then the same slope in a regression that also contains the log of the agent's mean answer length (game fixed effects, SEs clustered by episode). Length per unit c: the change in answer length per unit coefficient.Games played for these results9: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), harvest_5p, harvest_5p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read itIf 100% of the shift remains with length held fixed, length explains none of it. A low share means steering and the readout both move with length: the readout partly measures verbosity. This is a statistical control, not proof — length can itself be part of a persona (an assertive agent is brief).
Result
  • Holding answer length fixed keeps ≥ 80% of the readout shift for 8 of 8 traits.

21. Group size and collective steering

QuestionDoes one steered agent matter less in a bigger group? And if every agent is steered, does the group change n times as much as with one?What is measuredTop: per game × trait of the one-agent condition, the steered agent's reward slope (as in section 9, SD units) and the co-players' readout slope (contagion, as in section 8), by the game's number of players. Bottom (games without hidden roles, where the total only says which side won): group welfare (everyone's total reward vs the unsteered episode with the same seed, as in section 7) per unit c, with one agent steered and with all steered; 'players × one' is what all-steered would give if each agent's effect simply added. The factors are least-squares ratios over all game × trait cells.Games played for these results7: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read itFactor ≈ players: effects add. ≈ 1: steering everyone does about what steering one does. Rows of the bottom table: cells where steering everyone significantly changes welfare.
Result
  • One steered agent's own reward effect shrinks with group size (rank correlation -0.47, p = 0.000); its contagion does not change measurably with group size (rank correlation +nan, p = nan) (56 game × trait cells).
  • Steering everyone changes group welfare by about 0.85× the effect of steering one agent. If each steered agent added its own effect, it would be players × as much; it is 0.26 of that: effects do not add up across agents (40 game × trait cells).
  • Where everyone steered does something one steered agent does not (all-steered effect > 3× the one-agent effect, and that one is not significant or has the other sign): gbs_6p (image) × opportunistic (one +0.00, all -0.26); gbs_6p × opportunistic (one -0.07, all -0.36); gbs_6p × sarcastic (one +0.01, all -0.17). A persona everyone shares can change the group's result where one agent with it does not.

22. Hidden-role games: who carries the persona, and what it does to who wins

QuestionIn Avalon, Mafia and Werewolf, does it matter whether the whole deceiving side carries the persona (evil_team), one deceiver (evil_one), the whole honest side (good_team), one honest player (good_one) or everyone (all)? Does the same pattern hold across the games?What is measuredPer episode, whether the deceiving side won (spies, mafia, werewolves; 'evil' is the game's name for that side, not the evil trait). a: win rate at each c per setting, pooled over the 8 traits, the prompt version of evil_team as squares and the unsteered rate at c = 0. b: win rate with the trait pushed up (all c > 0) minus pushed down (all c < 0), per trait. c: win rate at strong (|c| > 1) minus mild (|c| ≤ 1) steering, per side. d: the same trait and direction with a different carrier. e: the steered agent's own reward slope as deceiver vs honest player. Tests: two proportions over episodes, Benjamini–Hochberg over b, c and d together.Games played for these results2: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image)How to read itPositive = the deceivers win more. In b, a cell is a trait's net effect on who wins; read across a row to see whether it holds in every game. In c, negative on both sides = the side does worse the harder it is steered, whatever the direction (the curves in a bend down at both ends). Where the deceivers win nearly every unsteered game (first finding), effects can mostly only be losses.
Result
  • Unsteered, the deceivers win: avalon_6p (image) 33% (n = 39); avalon_6p 44% (n = 39).
  • Across games, of the traits whose up-vs-down difference is significant in some game, the direction is the same in every game for: good_team: 2 of 2 (assertive, trustworthiness); all: 0 of 1 (–).
  • Largest up-vs-down differences: avalon_6p (image) all × trustworthiness: -64 points; avalon_6p (image) good_team × trustworthiness: -38 points; avalon_6p good_team × assertive: -35 points.
  • Mirror (evil_team vs good_team, trait pushed up vs down, both significant): no game × trait is significant for both sides yet. 'Helps whichever side carries it' points to a persona that makes a team play better; 'favours one side whoever carries it' to a trait that matters through the game's roles.
  • Carrier: with the same trait and direction, the whole side vs one member differs significantly in 3 of 64 game × trait × direction cases, one deceiver vs one honest player in 0 of 32 (list d). Most comparisons show no difference at this sample size; of the differences, 0 of 3 are the larger or deceiving carrier losing more when the trait is pushed down.

24. Risk and tempo

QuestionBesides shifting the average outcome, does steering make outcomes more variable (riskier)? And do steered groups play faster or slower?What is measuredRisk: the standard deviation of the steered agent's reward change (one-agent persona vector, SD units, as in section 9) at each |c|, pooled, and per game × trait between the weakest and the strongest coefficient. Tempo: per episode with every agent steered, the log of the number of turns over the coefficient (game fixed effects; shown as % per unit c), and the share of episodes stopped at the turn limit at the strongest coefficient.Games played for these results9: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), harvest_5p, harvest_5p (image), iterated_ultimatum_2pHow to read itA rising SD = stronger steering makes the agent's results less predictable. Negative length = games end sooner (decisions faster, or an early loss).
Result
  • Spread of the reward change: SD 1.88 at |c| = 2, 1.88 at |c| = 2 (1.00×); it grows from the weakest to the strongest coefficient in 0 of 56 game × trait cells. Steering shifts outcomes; it does not make them more erratic.
  • Games change length by ≥ 3% per unit c when everyone is steered for: assertive (-4.2%); empathy (+4.3%); opportunistic (+7.7%). Unsteered games are cut off at the turn limit in 0.0% of cases.

25. Image vs text × vector vs prompt: slopes and synergy

QuestionDoes seeing the game as a picture change what steering does, game by game? Does it change the vector, the prompt and both alike? And do vector and prompt add up, in the language and in the result, with text and with images?What is measuredGames played both ways only (avalon_6p, gbs_3p, gbs_6p, harvest_5p). a: per game × trait the slope per unit c of the steered agent's readout of its trait (SD vs the game's unsteered agents) and of its reward change (same seat, same seed, unsteered; SD units), with text (x) and with images (y); persona vector, settings without a side. b: the dose curves those slopes summarise, with the fitted line drawn. c: one steered agent, vector (c = ±1), prompt and both (c = ±1) per mode, as in section 19. d: both − (vector + prompt) per mode, all three against the same unsteered reference. e: the same per game (every game with all three arms), and whether the games differ beyond their noise (Cochran's Q per trait × side × mode; for the language on the raw projection, which is comparable across games). Tests: image − text with independent SEs; Benjamini–Hochberg over each chart's or table's cells.Games played for these results8: avalon_6p, avalon_6p (image), gbs_3p, gbs_3p (image), gbs_6p, gbs_6p (image), harvest_5p, harvest_5p (image)How to read itIn a, dots on the dashed diagonal = the picture changes nothing; a tight cloud along it = steering transfers across modes game by game. In b, the dashed line is the slope: a curve far from its line (bends, plateaus) is summarised badly by one number (section 16). In d, 0 = the two channels add; on the readout, values below 0 can be a ceiling of the projection rather than competition.
Result
  • Slopes, image vs text, language (readout): per game × trait the slope with images correlates r = with the slope with text (n = 0); same sign in 0 of 0; significantly different (BH) in 0.
  • Slopes, image vs text, result (reward): per game × trait the slope with images correlates r = 0.58 with the slope with text (n = 24); same sign in 11 of 24; significantly different (BH) in 3: avalon_6p × trustworthiness (-0.02 with text, +0.11 with images), gbs_3p × assertive (+0.08 with text, +0.47 with images), gbs_3p × trustworthiness (+0.13 with text, -0.21 with images).
  • Channels by mode (pooled, intended way, SD): vector with text, with images; prompt with text, with images; both with text, with images.
  • Synergy, language: prompt + vector is more than the sum of the two in 0 (text) / 0 (images) of 16 trait × side cases, less in 0 / 0: in both modes they simply add.
  • Synergy, result: prompt + vector is more than the sum of the two in 0 (text) / 0 (images) of 16 trait × side cases, less in 0 / 0: in both modes they simply add.
  • Per game, language (table e): of 0 game × trait × side cells, prompt + vector is significantly more than the sum in 0 and less in 0 (BH over the table). Too few games per mode to test whether they differ.
  • Per game, result (table e): of 0 game × trait × side cells, prompt + vector is significantly more than the sum in 0 and less in 0 (BH over the table). Too few games per mode to test whether they differ.

e. Synergy per game

Every game with all three arms, text and image separately. Cell: both − (vector + prompt); colour by how certain (red = more than the sum, blue = less), stars: Benjamini–Hochberg over the table; hover for n and SE. Language values are in each game's own SD units, which differ a hundredfold between games: compare colours and stars across games, not the numbers.

Language: both − (vector + prompt), intended way (SD of the game's unsteered agents)

gameagreeableness +agreeableness −assertive +assertive −empathy +empathy −evil +evil −opportunistic +opportunistic −sarcastic +sarcastic −sycophantic +sycophantic −trustworthiness +trustworthiness −

Result: both − (vector + prompt) (SD)

gameagreeableness +agreeableness −assertive +assertive −empathy +empathy −evil +evil −opportunistic +opportunistic −sarcastic +sarcastic −sycophantic +sycophantic −trustworthiness +trustworthiness −

Per game

What you seeEach game separately, one row per trait. Readout: the vector's slope on the steered agents' trait readout (SD per unit c; section 2) and the mean readout with the persona prompt + / − (SD). Outcomes, in the game's own reward units, paired with the same seat in the unsteered episode with the same seed: the steered agent's reward per unit c (vector, section 9); the one prompted agent's mean reward change (prompt + / −); the group's total reward per unit c when every agent gets the vector (welfare); in hidden-role games the deceiving side's reward per unit c when all its members get the vector. Below each game, by setting: the same reward slope for every setting (who is steered: one, half, all, one side, the random control, the prompt), for the steered agents and for the unsteered co-players of the same episodes.How to read itSlopes carry stars after Benjamini–Hochberg correction over the game's table; prompt columns are means ± 95% CI. The unsteered line gives the scale: e.g. a win/loss game with reward 0/1 has mean reward = win rate, so a slope of 0.1 = +10 percentage points of wins per unit c.
